source.title: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models
source.authors: Hugo Touvron; Thibaut Lavril; Gautier Izacard; X. Martinet; M. Lachaux; Timothée Lacroix; Baptiste Rozière; Naman Goyal; Eric Hambro; Faisal Azhar; Aurélien Rodriguez; A. Joulin; E. Grave; Guillaume Lample

record.tranche_reason: Reports downstream benchmark performance over training for LLaMA models and relates it to training perplexity, using a different measurement from the scaling-law claims. It does not fit or test held-out-loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports training loss over tokens in Figure 1, not held-out loss, and does not fit power laws or assess prediction from smaller runs. Its downstream results in benchmark tables compare models of different sizes; the training-trajectory evidence most directly addressing downstream predictability is Figure 2. It does not test compute-optimal allocations or architecture variation at fixed parameter count.
record.test_reason: This is a model-release paper, not a scaling-law study. Its only result bearing on a version is Section 3.7 and Figure 2: downstream accuracy tracked over training tokens for four sizes. The authors say this accuracy 'correlates with the training perplexity', with named exceptions. That is qualitative evidence on V6, in the new setting of training well past Chinchilla-optimal token counts (1.0–1.4T tokens). No power-law fits, held-out loss curves, extrapolation or allocation experiments are reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors' main conclusions concern public-data training and efficiency: LLaMA-13B beats GPT-3 and LLaMA-65B is competitive with Chinchilla and PaLM. On scale, they say smaller models trained on more tokens than Chinchilla recommends keep improving: the 7B model improves beyond 1T tokens. They report 'a constant improvement in performance as we were scaling'. Downstream accuracy during training mostly correlates with training perplexity, with SIQA and WinoGrande as exceptions.
record.recipe_differences: Trains and evaluates the LLaMA model series rather than fitting the original studies' scaling-law formulations; reports training loss and downstream benchmark trajectories, not held-out-loss power-law fits.
record.method_sensitivity: Benchmark choice changes the reported trajectory: SIQA is variable and WinoGrande correlates less well with training perplexity.
record.problems: The training-trajectory plots provide no tabulated numerical values or uncertainty estimates. Training loss is reported rather than held-out loss, and the paper does not fit or evaluate predictions from scaling laws.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports numerous cross-model downstream benchmark comparisons in Tables 3–10, plus other benchmark results during training in Figure 2. These were not separately extracted; the selected rows capture the text's explicit aggregate description and its named exceptions for the training-trajectory evidence relevant to V6.

untested.parts: No held-out loss and no power-law fit. Fig. 1 shows only training loss for four sizes.
No fitting on small runs and no prediction of larger runs.
No compute-optimal allocation experiment. The 7B model 'continues to improve even after 1T tokens', but this does not test the loss-minimising split at fixed compute.
No architecture variation at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or regimes. The single instruction-finetuning experiment does not vary scale.
No quantitative predictive mapping from scale or loss to downstream scores, and no held-out loss. The cross-size benchmark tables are not linked to rows.
No fitting choices or exponents examined.

record.verdict_notes: The cross-size tables (Tables 3–9) are declared in rows_left_out, but they contain non-monotonic cases relevant to V6 that a reviewer may want as rows. Examples: ARC-c 33B 57.8 vs 65B 56.0; ARC-e 80.0 vs 78.9; NQ 0-shot 24.9 vs 23.8; OBQA 7B 57.2 vs 13B 56.4. Toxicity (Table 11) rises with size, which is not a version of this claim. Tranche changed from T2 to T3 because the paper does not aim at the scaling question; its evidence comes incidentally from a new over-trained setting.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss and power-law fits across parameters, tokens, or compute.
Fitting on small runs and testing predictions on substantially larger runs.
Loss-minimising parameter and token allocations under fixed compute, and their scaling with compute.
Architecture comparisons at a fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The paper reports downstream performance over training and its relation to training perplexity, but does not fit a predictive mapping from pretraining loss or scale to downstream outcomes.
Sensitivity of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocations to setup and fitting choices; departures from fitted power laws.

rows.subject: LLaMA models (7B, 13B, 33B, 65B)
rows.operation_detail: Tracked downstream benchmark performance during training as token count increased.
rows.measure: Accuracy during training; authors describe performance as improving steadily on most benchmarks and correlating with training perplexity.
rows.note: Aggregate trajectory for the LLaMA model series; the paper gives a verbal description rather than numerical points.
rows.check: The value is a figure trajectory plus a verbal statement only. 'Correlates with training perplexity' is asserted, not quantified, and the perplexity is training loss (Fig. 1), not held-out loss. Observed holds only for qualitative steady improvement, not for a fitted predictive mapping.

rows.subject: LLaMA models (7B, 13B, 33B, 65B)
rows.operation_detail: Tracked downstream benchmark performance during training as token count increased.
rows.measure: Accuracy during training; authors report considerable variance in performance.
rows.note: The authors identify SIQA as an exception to the generally steady performance improvement.
rows.check: The authors attribute the SIQA variance to the benchmark possibly being 'not reliable'. That points to measurement noise rather than unpredictability of the model. Partial is acceptable, but note this attribution.

rows.subject: LLaMA models (7B, 13B, 33B, 65B)
rows.operation_detail: Tracked downstream benchmark performance during training as token count increased.
rows.measure: Accuracy during training; authors report that performance does not correlate as well with training perplexity, and that LLaMA-33B and LLaMA-65B perform similarly during training.
rows.note: The authors identify WinoGrande as an exception to the general correlation with training perplexity.
rows.check: Correct as recorded: on WinoGrande, 33B and 65B perform similarly during training despite differing training loss. The text says it 'does not correlate as well with training perplexity'.

relationships.condition: TriviaQA, NaturalQuestions, HellaSwag, PIQA training trajectories, LLaMA 7B–65B
relationships.reason: The authors state accuracy improves steadily and correlates with training perplexity (r1–r4). Evidence is qualitative and figure-only.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy improved steadily across the evaluated training trajectories and correlated with training perplexity.

relationships.reason: SIQA shows large variance (r5). On WinoGrande, 33B and 65B track similarly despite different training loss (r6), so loss does not predict the score there.
relationships.display_finding: SIQA trajectories varied substantially, while 33B and 65B tracked similarly on WinoGrande despite different training losses.
